lines.text: Ananya pastes a job description into her script and asks: tell me about this job.
Back comes a friendly paragraph. But a program is reading this reply, so prose is a bug.
The fix is not cleverer wording. A good prompt is a specification.
Start with a role and one clear task: you extract job details from a job description.
Add constraints: what to do when information is missing. If the CTC is not stated, use null. Never guess.
Then spell out the exact output: JSON, with a role, a list of skills, and the CTC.
Rules live in the system prompt. The job description goes in the user message, wrapped in tags, as data.
So if that text says, ignore your instructions, it is less likely to work.
Next, show one or two examples of a perfect answer. That is few-shot prompting: the model copies the pattern.
Turn on JSON mode, and the reply parses as JSON. But valid JSON can still be wrong: here, the CTC came back as a word.
So check every reply against a schema. If it fails, send the error back and ask once more.
And treat prompts like code: keep versions, and rerun a few real test cases after every change.
Write the prompt like a spec. Then validate what comes back, before your code trusts it.
